title: Protective anti‐prion antibodies in human immunoglobulin repertoires
abstract: Prion immunotherapy may hold great potential, but antibodies against certain PrP epitopes can be neurotoxic. Here, we identified > 6,000 PrP-binding antibodies in a synthetic human Fab phage display library, 49 of which we characterized in detail. Antibodies directed against the flexible tail of PrP conferred neuroprotection against infectious prions. We then mined published repertoires of circulating B cells from healthy humans and found antibodies similar to the protective phage-derived antibodies. When expressed recombinantly, these antibodies exhibited anti-PrP reactivity. Furthermore, we surveyed 48,718 samples from 37,894 hospital patients for the presence of anti-PrP IgGs and found 21 high-titer individuals. The clinical files of these individuals did not reveal any enrichment of specific pathologies, suggesting that anti-PrP autoimmunity is innocuous. The existence of anti-prion antibodies in unbiased human immunological repertoires suggests that they might clear nascent prions early in life. Combined with the reported lack of such antibodies in carriers of disease-associated PRNP mutations, this suggests a link to the low incidence of spontaneous prion diseases in human populations.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2020 EMBO Molecular Medicine article has attracted steady scholarly attention, with 24 citations in OpenAlex and a high field- and year-normalized percentile standing. Its influence is concentrated in prion research and adjacent areas of neurodegeneration, antibody science, and amyloidosis, while downstream reuse also includes reviews, book chapters, and preprints. The record shows early public visibility as well, including two news items and a small amount of community discussion, alongside one PubPeer thread that indicates post-publication scrutiny.

Full narrative

The article addresses a therapeutically important problem in prion biology: how to identify antibodies that may protect against infectious prions without triggering the neurotoxicity associated with some PrP epitopes. In the reported work, the authors screened a synthetic human Fab phage display library, characterized a subset of PrP-binding antibodies in detail, and then connected those findings to antibodies present in published repertoires of circulating B cells from healthy humans. The central scientific contribution is a mechanistic and translational one: antibodies targeting the flexible tail of PrP were associated with neuroprotection, suggesting a path toward safer prion immunotherapy.

The article’s citation pattern suggests that it has been taken up as part of an active and specialized research conversation rather than as a broad, general reference. Citing work is concentrated in prion disease and protein misfolding, with additional reach into neurological disease, amyloidosis, and antibody research. The venues citing it include both field-facing journals and preprints, which points to use in ongoing work as well as in synthesized overviews. Recent citing papers include a 2025 book chapter on therapeutic trajectories in human prion diseases and a 2026 status update on multi-target approaches to prion drug discovery, indicating that the paper continues to be relevant in forward-looking discussions of treatment strategy.

Public and community signals are modest but present. Crossref event data records two news items discussing the article soon after publication, including coverage on ScienceDaily and EurekAlert, and the social record includes a Hypothesis annotation tied to EMBO press materials about transparent peer review. These signals do not substitute for citations, but they show that the work drew attention beyond the journal page. The reuse graph also shows 25 documented downstream reuse events, including articles, preprints, book chapters, and a review, reinforcing that the paper has been incorporated into the broader literature.

At the same time, the record is not especially dense in post-publication commentary: scite reports mostly mentioning citations, with only two supporting statements, and there is one PubPeer thread. That combination suggests a paper that is being used and discussed, but with relatively limited visible debate in the captured sources. The article is openly accessible and indexed in multiple repositories, which likely helped its reach, and its funding and institutional footprint is centered on the University of Zurich with additional support from Swiss and industry funders. Overall, the evidence points to a focused but meaningful contribution: a prion-immunology study that has become part of the technical and translational literature on antibody-based approaches to neurodegenerative protein misfolding.
